cases.holding: Answering certified questions from the Second Circuit, the Court of Appeals held that a child's exposure to domestic violence does not alone establish neglect or justify removal, that neglect requires a preponderance showing of actual or imminent impairment caused by the parent's failure to exercise a minimum degree of care, and that emergency removal without a court order under Family Court Act § 1024 is permissible only where the danger is so urgent that there is no time to obtain an ex parte order.
cases.quote: emergency removal is appropriate where the danger is so immediate, so urgent that the child's life or safety will be at risk before an ex parte order can be obtained

relevance.INP-03: Police and agency referrals arising from domestic-violence calls cannot, standing alone, be treated as establishing danger to the child under this decision.
relevance.INP-04: When a court directs or reviews child-protective intervention, Nicholson supplies the statutory neglect elements the court must find.
relevance.INP-12: Nicholson sets the governing New York standard for taking a child into protective custody without prior judicial authorization.
relevance.DEC-04: This is the controlling New York authority on when an agency may remove a child before obtaining a court order.
relevance.DEC-05: Nicholson defines the two elements (impairment or imminent danger, plus failure to exercise a minimum degree of care) an article 10 petition must plead and prove.
relevance.DEC-06: The Court rejected any blanket presumption favoring removal and required consideration of less intrusive alternatives, which is the doctrinal basis for non-court service responses.
relevance.ACT-03: Foster placement must rest on particularized evidence of imminent risk and on the balance between the harm of remaining home and the harm of removal.
relevance.ACT-05: Nicholson identifies court-ordered exclusion of the offending adult as an alternative to removing the child from the home.
relevance.OUT-01: The decision requires courts to weigh the trauma of continued separation, reinforcing return home as the default where imminent risk is absent.
relevance.FAIL-02: A removal that does not satisfy the § 1024 imminent-danger and no-time-to-apply conditions is unlawful under New York law.
relevance.FAIL-05: The Court rejected practices that charged battered mothers with neglect merely for being victims, the paradigm New York claim of discriminatory agency action.

cases.case_name: Matter of Lee TT. v. Dowling
cases.holding: The Court of Appeals held that the 'some credible evidence' standard for retaining an indicated report in the Statewide Central Register violates federal due process to the extent the report is disseminated to provider and licensing agencies, and that a subject is entitled to a pre-deprivation hearing at which the agency must prove the abuse or maltreatment by a fair preponderance of the evidence.
cases.quote: subjects are entitled to a predeprivation hearing to determine by a fair preponderance of the evidence whether reports of abuse can be substantiated and relevant to future employment or licensure

relevance.INP-01: The opinion sets out the mandated-reporter framework of Social Services Law §§ 413-414 that feeds the Central Register.
relevance.INP-02: It confirms that permissive reports from any person, identified or anonymous, enter the same register and trigger the same consequences.
relevance.INP-06: Anonymous hotline reports are expressly within the intake scheme the Court describes and constrains.
relevance.INP-10: The decision describes the statutory test for transmitting a hotline report to the local agency for investigation.
relevance.DEC-01: Unfounded reports must be deleted and destroyed under the scheme the Court construes here.
relevance.DEC-02: It identifies the statutory threshold that converts an accepted report into a local child-protective investigation.
relevance.DEC-03: This is the leading New York authority on the evidentiary standard and hearing rights attaching to a substantiated (indicated) finding.
relevance.FAIL-01: The Court annulled agency determinations made under an unconstitutional standard, the model for judicial reversal of a substantiation.
relevance.FAIL-06: It limits when register information may be released and to whom, defining unlawful disclosure.
relevance.PMC-05: The opinion delineates the confidentiality and controlled-disclosure regime governing child-abuse records in New York.

cases.holding: Affirming findings of abuse and an order of supervision, the Court held that Family Court Act § 1046(a)(ii) creates only a rebuttable presumption shifting the burden of going forward to the respondents, while the burden of proving abuse by a preponderance always remains with the petitioning agency.
cases.quote: The establishment of a prima facie case does not require the court to find that the parents were culpable; it merely establishes a rebuttable presumption of parental culpability

relevance.INP-04: The decision governs how courts evaluate unexplained medical findings referred for child-protective adjudication.
relevance.INP-07: An unexplained sexually transmitted infection diagnosed in a medical setting is treated as evidence of abuse under § 1046(a)(ii).
relevance.DEC-03: It fixes the burden of proof and the evidentiary weight of a res ipsa-style prima facie case behind a founded finding.
relevance.DEC-05: Agencies filing article 10 petitions may rely on § 1046(a)(ii) but retain the burden of persuasion throughout.
relevance.ACT-02: The disposition was a twelve-month order of supervision with counseling, illustrating court-ordered services short of removal.
relevance.ACT-06: The Court weighed the parents' failure to obtain treatment and retesting for their children as evidence bearing on culpability.
relevance.OUT-05: Because the presumption is rebuttable, a respondent who defeats it is entitled to dismissal of the petition.

cases.holding: The Court affirmed dismissal of neglect petitions, holding that parents who sought accredited medical assistance and chose a treatment recommended by a duly licensed physician and not totally rejected by all responsible medical authority have not failed to supply adequate medical care.
cases.quote: have provided for their child a treatment which is recommended by their physician and which has not been totally rejected by all responsible medical authority

relevance.INP-05: A family that voluntarily engages medical providers and follows a licensed physician's plan is not thereby exposed to a neglect finding.
relevance.INP-07: It sets the limit on when a treating physician's disagreement with parental choices converts a medical encounter into medical neglect.
relevance.DEC-06: The deference owed to parental medical judgment supports resolving such cases without a court petition where an acceptable course of treatment exists.
relevance.ACT-01: Voluntary parental engagement with accredited care is the benchmark the Court used to reject compelled state intervention.
relevance.ACT-06: This is the leading New York authority on when the State may override parental medical decision-making for a child.

cases.holding: The Court affirmed termination of parental rights for permanent neglect, holding that the agency must first prove diligent efforts and that the parent failed to maintain contact with or plan for the child for more than a year, and that at the separate dispositional hearing the child's best interests control with no presumption favoring return to the parent.
cases.quote: the threshold inquiry by the court in any neglect proceeding must be whether the agency exercised diligent efforts to strengthen the parental relationship

relevance.ACT-02: The opinion enumerates the statutory service obligations - counseling, visitation, assistance with housing and employment - that a court-ordered plan must contain.
relevance.OUT-01: Diligent efforts to reunite the family are a precondition to any termination, making reunification the presumptive first path.
relevance.OUT-02: This is the leading New York statement of the permanent-neglect elements and of the two-stage fact-finding then best-interests structure of a termination trial.

cases.holding: The Court held that an agency seeking termination for permanent neglect must affirmatively plead in detail and prove by clear and convincing evidence that it exercised diligent efforts to strengthen the parent-child relationship, and that failure to carry that threshold burden requires dismissal of the petition as to that parent.
cases.quote: It has declared as a matter of public policy that the State may not intervene to terminate a parent's rights when assistance in strengthening the family has not been forthcoming

relevance.ACT-01: The Court catalogues the assistance - counseling, visitation, housing and employment help - an agency must offer before a parent's conduct can be judged.
relevance.ACT-02: It converts the statutory diligent-efforts guidelines into an enforceable, case-specific service obligation on the agency.
relevance.OUT-01: Agency failure to work toward reunification bars termination regardless of the parent's own shortcomings.
relevance.OUT-02: Diligent efforts are a necessary prerequisite, pleaded in detail and proved by clear and convincing evidence, to any permanent-neglect finding.
relevance.FAIL-01: The Court reinstated Family Court's dismissal, reversing an appellate ruling that had excused the agency's failures.

cases.holding: The Court held that awarding custody to foster parents under Social Services Law § 392(6) was impermissible and that the best-interests inquiry for a child in temporary foster care compares continued foster care against discharge to the biological parent or other relative or suitable person, rather than measuring parent against foster parent.
cases.quote: analysis of the child's "best interest" must begin not by measuring biological parent against foster parent but by weighing past and continued foster care against discharge to the biological parent

relevance.INP-05: The Court emphasizes that parents in temporary crisis are encouraged to place children voluntarily under § 384-a without forfeiting their rights.
relevance.DEC-06: Voluntary placement with services, rather than a coercive petition, is the statutory path the Court describes for families in temporary crisis.
relevance.ACT-01: Social Services Law § 384-a voluntary placement is framed here as a service to families, not an admission of unfitness.
relevance.ACT-03: Foster care is characterized as a temporary way station, not a permanent condition or a competing custodial claim.
relevance.ACT-04: Section 392(6) directs discharge to the parent or to another relative or suitable person before continued foster care is ordered.
relevance.OUT-01: The State's first obligation is to reunite the family, and diligent efforts must continue while the child is in care.
relevance.OUT-02: Termination requires clear and convincing proof of a statutory ground, and a suspended judgment gives a strictly time-limited second chance.
relevance.OUT-03: Where a child has bonded with a non-parent caregiver, continued placement may be appropriate even without a finding of parental unfitness.

cases.holding: The Court affirmed terminations of the parental rights of incarcerated fathers, holding that although incarceration alone is not a ground for termination and the parent's special circumstances must be considered, a plan consisting only of indefinite long-term foster care for the duration of the child's minority does not satisfy the statutory planning requirement.
cases.quote: an incarcerated parent may not satisfy the planning requirement of the statute where the only plan offered is long-term foster care lasting potentially for the child's entire minority

relevance.OUT-02: This is the controlling New York authority on permanent neglect and termination where the parent is incarcerated.
relevance.OUT-04: The Court holds that foster care may not be used as a permanent way of life extending through the child's entire minority.

cases.holding: Reversing and ordering a new hearing, the Court held that custody may be taken from a parent and given to a non-parent only on proof of surrender, abandonment, persisting neglect, unfitness, or other like extraordinary circumstances, and that only after extraordinary circumstances are shown may the court decide custody on the child's best interests.
cases.quote: The State may not deprive a parent of the custody of a child absent surrender, abandonment, persisting neglect, unfitness or other like extraordinary circumstances

relevance.ACT-04: Placement of a child with a relative or other non-parent caregiver over parental objection requires the extraordinary-circumstances threshold.
relevance.OUT-03: This is the foundational New York authority governing permanency through custody or guardianship with a non-parent.

cases.holding: The Court reversed a termination order, holding for the first time that the right to assigned counsel in proceedings to terminate parental rights necessarily includes the right to effective assistance, and that counsel who had never spoken with the parent before the fact-finding hearing and announced he would remain silent did not provide it.
cases.quote: the right to assigned counsel in proceedings to terminate parental rights necessarily encompasses the right to effective assistance of counsel

relevance.DEC-05: Once the State initiates a proceeding that can sever the parent-child relationship, an indigent parent's entitlement to counsel attaches and must be meaningful.
relevance.OUT-02: A termination entered after constitutionally ineffective representation cannot stand and must be reversed.
relevance.FAIL-01: This is the current New York authority for vacating an agency-sought order because of a procedural failure in the parent's representation.

cases.holding: The Court affirmed confirmation of an indicated Central Register report, holding that there is no constitutional right to assigned counsel at a Statewide Central Register administrative fair hearing and that the 2020 amendments to Social Services Law § 422 - including the fair-preponderance standard and the irrebuttable presumption from an article 10 dismissal - do not apply retroactively to determinations rendered before their January 1, 2022 effective date.
cases.quote: Inclusion on the SCR—unlike Family Court article 10 proceedings—does not impact rights that we have concluded warrant recognition of a constitutional right to assigned counsel in civil proceedings

relevance.INP-03: The report at issue originated from a police officer's referral to the Statewide Central Register after interviewing the child.
relevance.INP-06: It describes the register's function of informing child-care providers and licensors that a person has a substantiated report.
relevance.INP-10: The opinion traces the path from hotline report through local agency investigation to an indicated determination.
relevance.DEC-01: It explains that under prior law a Family Court dismissal created no presumption that the register record should be unfounded.
relevance.DEC-03: This is the current Court of Appeals decision on the procedural protections and evidentiary standard governing a substantiated finding.
relevance.FAIL-05: The Court acknowledges that the 2020 amendments were enacted to address disparities in outcomes for poor families and across racial lines, while holding them prospective only.

cases.holding: The Court held that no private right of action for money damages may be implied from title 4 or title 6 of article 6 of the Social Services Law for a child-welfare agency's failure to provide statutorily mandated services, because the Legislature enacted a comprehensive enforcement scheme centered on monitoring and loss of State reimbursement.
cases.quote: Recognition of such a private right of action under title 4 would not be consistent with the legislative scheme

relevance.INP-02: The Court reproduces the Social Services Law § 419 good-faith immunity provision covering reporting, investigation, and removal.
relevance.INP-09: Enforcement of New York's child-welfare service mandates runs through monitoring and fiscal penalties, not private suits.
relevance.OUT-06: Families of children harmed in agency care cannot base a damages claim on breach of the Social Services Law service mandates.
relevance.FAIL-03: This decision identifies withdrawal of State reimbursement as the Legislature's chosen remedy for a district's failure to meet statutory standards.
relevance.FAIL-04: It forecloses the statutory damages theory most often advanced after a child is seriously harmed while known to the system.
relevance.PMC-01: Performance failures are to be addressed through the statutory monitoring apparatus the Court describes rather than private enforcement.
relevance.PMC-02: Loss of State reimbursement to non-compliant local districts is the fiscal accountability mechanism the Court found exclusive.
relevance.PMC-04: Post-fatality accountability in New York must be pursued through the statutory oversight scheme rather than an implied statutory cause of action.

cases.case_name: Matter of Catherine G. v. County of Essex
cases.holding: The Court held that a fourteen-year-old sibling is not a 'person legally responsible' under Family Court Act § 1012, so mandated reporters had no statutory duty to report his abuse of his sisters and the mother's late notice of claim against county and school officials was patently meritless.
cases.quote: When in doubt about whether a case must be reported under Social Services Law § 413, they ought to err on the side of caution and make a report

relevance.INP-01: This decision fixes the outer boundary of the mandated-reporter duty by defining who can be the subject of a reportable allegation.
relevance.INP-02: It confirms that anyone may report, while limiting who may be named as a subject of a Central Register report.
relevance.INP-05: The mother's own calls to the hotline and disclosures to a pediatrician and school psychologist are the paradigm guardian self-report.
relevance.INP-06: The Court describes how the state hotline screened the mother's calls and accepted a later third-party report.
relevance.INP-08: A school psychologist's referral to counseling without a hotline report was held lawful because the alleged abuser was a sibling.
relevance.INP-10: The opinion shows the hotline's screening criteria determining whether a report is transmitted for investigation.
relevance.DEC-01: It validates screening out reports that do not allege conduct by a parent or person legally responsible.
relevance.DEC-02: The accepted third-party report produced a home visit and assessment, illustrating the investigation the statute contemplates.
relevance.OUT-05: The Court directed denial of leave to file a late notice of claim because the underlying claims were meritless.

cases.holding: Reversing the Appellate Division, the Court held that a municipality that assumes legal custody of a child by placing the child in foster care owes that child a common-law duty of care, so the plaintiff need not plead or prove a special duty to sue for negligent selection, retention, or supervision of the foster home.
cases.quote: municipalities owe a duty of care to the children the municipalities place in foster homes because the municipalities have assumed custody of those children

relevance.ACT-03: Placing a child in foster care creates an affirmative, enforceable duty of care owed by the placing municipality.
relevance.OUT-06: This is the controlling New York authority for a damages action by a child seriously harmed while in foster placement.
relevance.FAIL-04: It removes the special-duty pleading barrier that previously defeated most claims arising from harm to children in agency custody.
relevance.PMC-04: Civil liability for harm suffered in custody is now the principal New York mechanism for accountability after a foster-care tragedy.

cases.holding: The Court held that Family Court Act article 10-A confers no independent grant of continuing jurisdiction, so once an article 10 neglect petition is dismissed for failure to prove neglect the court loses subject matter jurisdiction and may not conduct further permanency hearings.
cases.quote: the dismissal of a neglect petition terminates Family Court's jurisdiction

relevance.INP-04: A court may not keep a child-welfare case open by judicial referral once the underlying petition has been dismissed.
relevance.ACT-02: Court-ordered supervision and services cannot survive dismissal of the petition that authorized them.
relevance.OUT-04: Continued permanency planning and placement past dismissal is unauthorized, which controls how youth remain in or exit care.
relevance.OUT-05: This is the leading New York authority on the jurisdictional consequences of dismissing an abuse or neglect petition.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: Reviewing New York's permanent-neglect scheme, the Supreme Court held that the fair-preponderance standard then prescribed by Family Court Act § 622 violates the Due Process Clause and that a State must support its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence before irrevocably severing parental rights.
cases.quote: the "fair preponderance of the evidence" standard prescribed by Fam. Ct. Act § 622 violates the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment

relevance.INP-11: Where a decision point turns on the federal constitutional floor rather than New York statute, Santosky supplies that floor for parental-rights cases.
relevance.OUT-02: This New York-origin decision fixes the constitutional burden of proof for every termination of parental rights.

cases.case_name: Smith v. Organization of Foster Families for Equality & Reform
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Supreme Court reversed, holding that without deciding whether foster parents have a constitutionally protected liberty interest, New York's pre-removal procedures under Social Services Law § 392 and New York City's SSC Procedure No. 5 are adequate to protect any such interest.
cases.quote: the procedures provided by New York State in § 392 and by New York City's SSC Procedure No. 5 are adequate to protect whatever liberty interests appellees may have

relevance.ACT-03: This decision defines the limited procedural rights that attach when a child is moved between foster placements in New York.
relevance.ACT-04: The Court notes that a natural parent of a child in voluntary placement retains an absolute right to return, constraining competing caregiver claims.
relevance.OUT-03: It addresses directly whether a long-term caregiver relationship can ripen into a constitutionally protected family interest.
relevance.FAIL-05: The opinion catalogues the criticisms of the foster system, including disparate treatment concerns, while confining the constitutional holding to procedure.

cases.case_name: Southerland v. City of New York
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit
cases.holding: The Second Circuit vacated summary judgment for the caseworker on the father's Fourth Amendment unlawful-search claim and the children's unlawful-seizure and procedural due process claims, holding that a Family Court order obtained on a materially misleading affidavit cannot supply the warrant equivalent and that fact disputes remained over whether emergency circumstances justified the removal.
cases.quote: In child-abuse investigations, a Family Court order is equivalent to a search warrant for Fourth Amendment purposes

relevance.INP-03: The case involves police officers accompanying a caseworker on a home entry and addresses the City's failure to train them.
relevance.INP-10: It shows what a caseworker must actually establish before escalating from a report to a court-authorized home search.
relevance.INP-12: Absent consent, a court order, or emergency circumstances, officials may not take children from a parent's custody.
relevance.DEC-02: A Family Court Act § 1034 investigative order is the Fourth Amendment warrant for a child-abuse home search and must rest on an accurate affidavit.
relevance.DEC-04: Whether emergency circumstances existed at the moment of removal is a fact question that defeats summary judgment where the record is disputed.
relevance.FAIL-02: The decision confirms that a procedural due process claim survives even where emergency circumstances existed, if no prompt post-deprivation hearing follows.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit
cases.holding: In an action arising from an infant's death and the ensuing child-protective proceeding, the Second Circuit held that agency lawyers who initiate and prosecute child-protective petitions have absolute immunity, that caseworkers have only qualified rather than absolute immunity, and that qualified immunity nonetheless barred the § 1983 claims against the caseworkers here.
cases.quote: The lawyer defendants are entitled to absolute immunity on plaintiffs § 1983 claims because they were performing functions analogous to those of a prosecutor

relevance.INP-03: Hospital and law-enforcement referrals following a child's death initiated the proceeding the court reviews.
relevance.DEC-05: Agency attorneys who file and prosecute an article 10 petition act in a prosecutorial function and are absolutely immune.
relevance.OUT-06: The decision arises from a contested child-fatality investigation and defines the immunities that follow it.
relevance.FAIL-02: Caseworkers who effect or seek a removal enjoy only qualified immunity, so an objectively unreasonable removal remains actionable.
relevance.FAIL-04: It shows the immunity defenses that confront families suing after a death investigation is mishandled.

cases.case_name: Doe v. New York City Department of Social Services
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit
cases.holding: The Second Circuit reversed entry of judgment notwithstanding the verdict, holding that a foster-care placement agency may be liable under § 1983 where its supervisory personnel exhibited deliberate indifference to a known risk of abuse and that failure proximately caused the child's injury.
cases.quote: we hold that entry of judgment n.o.v. for the defendant Bureau was unwarranted because the record contains sufficient evidence from which a jury could reasonably find deliberate indifference

relevance.OUT-06: It establishes that repeated warning signs ignored over years can support a jury verdict for a child seriously harmed in care.
relevance.FAIL-04: This is the foundational Second Circuit authority for agency liability when a child is abused while under supervision.
relevance.PMC-04: The court treats an agency's incomplete annual reporting of known concerns as evidence supporting deliberate indifference.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit
cases.holding: The Second Circuit affirmed certification of a Rule 23(b)(2) class of children in or at risk of entering New York City's child welfare system challenging systemic failures, while directing the district court to refine the class into subclasses before trial.
cases.quote: we hold that the district court did not abuse its discretion by certifying the class at this point in the litigation

relevance.INP-09: Systemic, class-wide litigation is the recognized vehicle in this circuit for forcing review of a child welfare system's performance.
relevance.FAIL-03: It permits aggregate challenges to a jurisdiction's failure to meet federal and state child-welfare obligations.
relevance.PMC-01: Class litigation supplements federal performance review as a mechanism for exposing and correcting systemic deficiencies.
relevance.PMC-02: Court-supervised structural relief provides the audit-like accounting that the statutory scheme alone does not compel.
relevance.PMC-03: Independent scrutiny of agency practice in this framework parallels the citizen-review function CAPTA contemplates.
relevance.PMC-06: Cross-cutting analysis of systemic weak points is precisely the kind of showing Rule 23(b)(2) certification permits here.

cases.case_name: Elisa W. v. City of New York
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit
cases.holding: The Second Circuit vacated the denial of class certification to children in New York City foster care alleging systemic deficiencies, holding that the district court applied an incorrect legal framework to commonality and typicality, and remanded for reconsideration of the class and subclasses.
cases.quote: The district court erred in its analysis of commonality and typicality under Rule 23

relevance.INP-09: The decision revives systemic oversight litigation as a route to scrutinize New York City's foster care administration.
relevance.FAIL-03: It rejects the view that discretionary, case-by-case agency decisions necessarily preclude a class-wide challenge to systemic failure.
relevance.PMC-01: Class-wide claims about safety, permanency, and well-being outcomes may proceed notwithstanding individual variation.
relevance.PMC-02: It keeps open the principal judicial mechanism for compelled system-wide accounting in New York City.
relevance.PMC-03: Independent review of agency practice can proceed through representative litigation where internal review does not.
relevance.PMC-06: Aggregated evidence of policy-level deficiencies is legally cognizable, not merely a collection of individual grievances.

cases.court: Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of the State of New York, Second Department
cases.holding: Reaching the merits under the mootness exception and reversing, the Second Department held that a parent excluded from the home by a full stay-away order of protection in an article 10 proceeding is entitled to a prompt Family Court Act § 1028 hearing applying the imminent-risk standard, because such an order is functionally equivalent to removal of the children from his care.
cases.quote: it must be governed by the same legal standards as are provided for removal of a child in Family Court Act §§ 1027 and 1028

relevance.INP-04: Judicially ordered exclusion from the home is an intervention of the same constitutional magnitude as taking the child into care.
relevance.INP-12: Separating parent and child by excluding the parent triggers the same protective-custody safeguards as physical removal.
relevance.DEC-04: The imminent-risk standard and three-court-day hearing right apply whichever side of the door the separation is accomplished from.
relevance.ACT-05: This is the leading published New York authority on the due process consequences of an exclusionary order of protection.
relevance.FAIL-01: The court reversed Family Court's denial of a § 1028 hearing and rejected contrary trial-level decisions.

cases.court: Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of the State of New York, First Department
cases.holding: The First Department held that Family Court may grant a suspended judgment retroactively after a parent has completed the terms of a dispositional order, vacating the neglect finding and dismissing the petition where that serves the children's best interests.
cases.quote: Family Court Act § 1051 (c) authorizes dismissal upon two separate and distinct grounds

relevance.ACT-02: Full compliance with a court-ordered service plan can be given retroactive effect to erase the underlying finding.
relevance.ACT-05: The children returned home only after the abusive partner was excluded, illustrating exclusion as the safety measure that permits reunification.
relevance.OUT-05: This is the published New York authority permitting vacatur of a neglect finding and dismissal after successful completion of services.

cases.court: Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of the State of New York, Second Department
cases.holding: The Second Department reversed, holding that Family Court Act § 1091 re-entry into foster care is available to any former foster care youth under twenty-one discharged for failing to consent to continued placement, including a youth originally placed following a person-in-need-of-supervision adjudication.
cases.quote: we conclude that Jefry was a "former foster care youth" within the meaning of Family Court Act § 1091

relevance.OUT-04: This is the leading published New York decision construing the article 10-B right of a youth who aged out to return to foster care before twenty-one.

cases.case_name: Kimberly S.M. v. Bradford Central School
cases.court: Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of the State of New York, Fourth Department
cases.holding: The Fourth Department reversed summary judgment and reinstated the complaint, holding that a mandated reporter's duty under Social Services Law § 413 is measured by the facts known when abuse is suspected and that liability under § 420(2) is not defeated merely because the alleged abuser later proves not to have been a person legally responsible for the child.
cases.quote: a mandated reporter is obligated to report suspected cases of child sexual abuse based upon facts and circumstances within the knowledge of the reporter

relevance.INP-01: This is the principal New York decision imposing civil liability on a mandated reporter for a willful failure to report.
relevance.INP-08: The reporter was a teacher, and the case defines what school staff must do when a student discloses abuse.

cases.court: Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of the State of New York, Third Department
cases.holding: The Third Department modified to dismiss the failure-to-report claims, holding that because a school employee who abused students was not a 'person legally responsible' for their care, the children were not 'abused children' for Social Services Law § 413 purposes and the school district could not be liable under § 420(2).
cases.quote: Civil liability may be imposed upon these individuals who knowingly and willfully fail to make the requisite report

relevance.INP-01: It states the § 413 duty and the § 420(2) liability standard while confining both to abuse by a parent or person legally responsible.
relevance.INP-08: This is the current Third Department authority on school-district exposure for failing to report abuse by a staff member.

cases.court: Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of the State of New York, Second Department
cases.holding: The Second Department held that Social Services Law § 419 immunity required dismissal of the complaint against the hospital that reported suspected child abuse, since a person or institution participating in good faith in making a report is immune from civil and criminal liability and good faith is presumed for mandated reporters.
cases.quote: We find, contrary to Special Term, that, by virtue of Social Services Law § 419, the foregoing complaint must be dismissed insofar as it is asserted against the defendant hospital

relevance.INP-01: Section 419 immunity and its presumption of good faith are the protection that makes the mandatory reporting duty workable.
relevance.INP-02: The same statutory immunity extends to any person or institution reporting in good faith, not only mandated reporters.
relevance.INP-07: This is the New York authority shielding hospitals and treating clinicians who report suspected abuse from retaliatory suit.

cases.case_name: Matter of Elizabeth B. v. New York State Office of Children & Family Services
cases.court: Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of the State of New York, Third Department
cases.holding: The Third Department annulled the portion of the OCFS determination that maintained an indicated report of inadequate guardianship against a mother who was herself the victim of domestic violence, ordering the report unfounded, expunged and sealed, because the minimum-degree-of-care inquiry must account for the risks and constraints she actually faced.
cases.quote: Respondent misconstrues this standard as one that cannot be "modified or excused because a parent is under stress or fear."

relevance.DEC-01: A report that cannot survive this analysis must be amended to unfounded, expunged and sealed.
relevance.DEC-03: It applies the fair-preponderance maltreatment standard and Nicholson's minimum-degree-of-care test to an administrative substantiation.
relevance.FAIL-01: This is a current example of an article 78 court annulling an agency substantiation on the merits.
relevance.FAIL-05: It rejects the practice of indicating battered parents for maltreatment on the basis of their own victimization.

cases.holding: The Court affirmed abuse findings in two proceedings, holding that as amended Family Court Act § 1046(a)(vi) permits a child's out-of-court statements to be corroborated by any other evidence tending to support their reliability, including validation testimony by a qualified expert and the cross-corroborating statements of other child victims.
cases.quote: As amended, section 1046 (a) (vi) states a broad flexible rule providing that out-of-court statements may be corroborated by "[a]ny other evidence tending to support" their reliability

relevance.DEC-03: This is the controlling New York rule on the corroboration required before a child's hearsay disclosure can support a founded finding.
relevance.DEC-05: Agencies petitioning on the strength of a child's disclosures must be prepared to supply corroboration meeting this standard.

cases.case_name: Matter of Lawyers for Children v. New York State Office of Children & Family Services
cases.citation: 2025 NY Slip Op 02115 (N.Y. App. Div. 3d Dep't Apr. 10, 2025)
cases.court: Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of the State of New York, Third Department
cases.holding: Over a dissent, the Third Department affirmed dismissal of an article 78 challenge to OCFS's Host Family Home regulations, holding that OCFS did not exceed its authority because the program is a preventive service in which the parent, not the State, decides whether and with whom to place the child.
cases.quote: Petitioners' argument that OCFS exceeded its authority when it created the Host Family Home program is unpersuasive

relevance.INP-05: The program exists precisely for parents who ask for help before any allegation, and the parent retains the placement decision.
relevance.INP-09: The case is the current test of whether an administrative child-welfare program can be created without legislation, litigated by an oversight organization.
relevance.DEC-06: This is the closest New York analogue to an alternative-response track: services arranged outside the court and foster care systems.
relevance.ACT-01: The opinion sets out OCFS's statutory authority to define and provide preventive services to avert formal child-welfare intervention.
relevance.ACT-04: It recites the statutory prioritization of kinship placement and sibling placement together under Social Services Law § 384-a(1-a).
relevance.FAIL-06: The court noted that the record's OCFS communications came from a Freedom of Information Law request and declined to treat them as authoritative or complete.
relevance.PMC-03: A children's legal-services organization performing an external watchdog role is the petitioner, testing agency rulemaking in court.

cases.case_name: Matter of New York Civ. Liberties Union v. City of Rochester
cases.holding: The Court of Appeals affirmed, holding that FOIL's personal privacy exemption does not permit an agency to withhold categorically all disciplinary records relating to unsubstantiated complaints; the agency must review each record individually and articulate a particularized and specific justification, disclosing with redactions where redaction would prevent an unwarranted invasion of privacy.
cases.quote: Public Officers Law § 87 (2) requires an agency to evaluate each record individually and determine whether "a particularized and specific justification" exists for denying access

relevance.FAIL-06: Blanket refusal to release records of unsubstantiated complaints is unlawful under New York's disclosure law.
relevance.PMC-05: This is the Court of Appeals' current statement of the record-by-record, particularized-justification rule governing FOIL requests to New York agencies.
relevance.PMC-06: It secures the underlying record access on which independent cross-analysis of agency performance depends.

cases.holding: The Court affirmed a termination of an incarcerated father's parental rights and held that, absent legislative authorization, Family Court has no power to order post-termination contact or visitation as a condition of a dispositional order in a contested Social Services Law § 384-b proceeding.
cases.quote: Absent legislative warrant, Family Court is not authorized to include any such condition in a dispositional order made pursuant to Social Services Law § 384-b

relevance.OUT-03: It marks the boundary between adoption, which severs legal ties entirely, and arrangements preserving contact, which require a voluntary agreement or statute.

cases.case_name: Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians v. Holyfield
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Supreme Court reversed, holding that 'domicile' under the Indian Child Welfare Act is a matter of uniform federal law, that children born off-reservation to reservation-domiciled parents were domiciled on the reservation, and that the tribal court therefore had exclusive jurisdiction under 25 U.S.C. § 1911(a), voiding the state adoption decree.
cases.quote: In enacting the ICWA Congress confirmed that, in child custody proceedings involving Indian children domiciled on the reservation, tribal jurisdiction was exclusive as to the States

relevance.INP-11: This is the controlling federal authority on when an Indian child's case must go to tribal court and when state jurisdiction is merely presumptively transferable, the standard New York courts must apply because no published New York appellate decision reaches ICWA's merits.

cases.court: Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of the State of New York, First Department
cases.holding: Reversing Family Court and granting the Tohono O'odham Nation's motion to intervene, the First Department held that the judicially created 'existing Indian family' exception cannot be engrafted onto the Indian Child Welfare Act, because the Act's only threshold requirements are that the matter be a child custody proceeding involving an Indian child, and remanded for a hearing on the 25 U.S.C. § 1915 placement preferences and any good cause to depart from them.
cases.quote: judicial insertion of an additional criterion for applicability is plainly beyond the intent of Congress and must be rejected

relevance.INP-11: This is the published New York appellate decision reaching ICWA's merits: it holds the Act applies whenever the child is a tribal member or eligible for membership regardless of the family's cultural ties, recognizes the tribe's independent right to intervene, and requires a hearing on the statutory placement preferences.

cases.holding: The Court held that an indigent parent charged with child neglect is entitled to assigned counsel and must be affirmatively advised of that right, so that a mother told only that she could hire and pay for a lawyer herself could not validly waive counsel or admit the petition, and it remitted the matter to Family Court for a new adjudicatory and dispositional hearing with counsel.
cases.quote: to be relinquished to the State without the opportunity for a hearing, with assigned counsel if the parent lacks the means to retain a lawyer

relevance.INP-04: When a neglect proceeding is opened against a parent, the court itself must advise the parent of the right to assigned counsel before taking any admission or proceeding to adjudication.
relevance.DEC-05: This is the foundational New York holding that filing an article 10 petition against an indigent parent triggers an enforceable right to assigned counsel, the right later extended to effective assistance in Matter of Parker J.

cases.case_name: Matter of Nassau County Dep't of Social Servs. ex rel. Dante M. v. Denise J.
cases.holding: The Court held that a newborn's positive toxicology for a controlled substance cannot by itself support a neglect finding because it does not establish the causative connection to actual or imminent impairment that Family Court Act § 1012(f)(i)(B) requires, but affirmed the findings and the one-year order of supervision because other evidence - prematurity, low birth weight, intensive-care and high-risk follow-up needs, and the mother's cocaine use during pregnancy - showed imminent danger of impairment to both children.
cases.quote: We conclude that more than a positive toxicology is generally required for a neglect determination.

relevance.INP-07: A hospital toxicology screen at birth is the classic medical disclosure, and this decision fixes how far that single laboratory result can carry an agency.
relevance.DEC-03: This is the leading New York causation authority for a founded finding: the agency must link the medical result to actual or imminent impairment rather than treat the result itself as the finding.
relevance.ACT-02: The Court approved a one-year order of supervision as the appropriate level of State intervention where the proof showed risk but no basis for removal.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit
cases.holding: The Second Circuit reversed directed verdicts for city child-welfare officials and the placement agencies and remanded for a new trial, holding that a mother and her children were deprived of their constitutionally protected right to family integrity without due process where the Bureau of Child Welfare took and then kept the children for years without her consent, without a court order, and without any hearing, and that § 1983 damages liability was for the jury.
cases.quote: the right of the family to remain together without the coercive interference of the awesome power of the state

relevance.INP-05: The mother placed her children informally only because she sought hospital treatment for herself, and this case holds that a parent who asks for help does not thereby forfeit custody.
relevance.INP-12: Taking and retaining custody of a child without parental consent and without court authorization violates the reciprocal due process rights of parent and child.
relevance.DEC-04: It is the foundational Second Circuit statement that state assumption of custody must be justified by consent, court order or genuine emergency, and cannot simply continue indefinitely.
relevance.FAIL-02: This is the case on which Tenenbaum and Southerland build: a custody deprivation effected and maintained without process is actionable under § 1983 against the responsible officials.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit
cases.holding: Reviewing the preliminary injunction against New York City's practice of removing children from mothers who had been battered, the Second Circuit held that the removals may raise serious federal constitutional questions but that antecedent, unsettled questions about the Family Court Act had to be answered first, and it therefore certified three questions to the New York Court of Appeals - on the definition of neglect, on whether witnessing domestic abuse is 'danger' or 'risk' to life or health, and on whether removal requires additional particularized evidence - retaining jurisdiction over the appeal.
cases.quote: We agree that in some circumstances the removals may raise serious questions of federal constitutional law. We conclude, however, that uncertain issues of state law precede our own constitutional inquiry.

relevance.INP-12: The certified questions frame the federal constraints on taking a child into protective custody in a domestic-violence household and identify the state-law predicates that must be settled before those constraints are applied.
relevance.DEC-04: This is the federal decision that produced the certification answered in Nicholson v. Scoppetta, 3 N.Y.3d 357, and it records the Second Circuit's view that a blanket presumption in favor of removal may not fairly capture the nuances of each family situation.

cases.holding: The Court affirmed findings of severe abuse and termination of parental rights, holding that the Adoption and Safe Families Act amendments applied to the pending proceedings, that the agency was properly excused from exercising diligent efforts at reunification given the aggravated circumstances, and that derivative findings of severe abuse may be made as to siblings who were not themselves the direct victims.
cases.quote: We conclude that an underlying finding that a child was abused may itself be derivative, even in cases other than those involving homicide or assault.

relevance.DEC-05: An article 10 petition may plead abuse or severe abuse derivatively as to every child in the household, so the agency need not allege a separate act against each sibling.
relevance.OUT-01: It supplies the statutory exception the reunification cases otherwise omit: diligent efforts to reunite are not required where a court finds aggravated circumstances or that such efforts would be detrimental to the child's best interests.

cases.holding: The Court affirmed a finding of severe abuse against a father, holding that the phrase 'circumstances evincing a depraved indifference to human life' in Social Services Law § 384-b(8)(a)(i) does not carry its Penal Law meaning, that § 384-b(8)(a)(iv)'s diligent-efforts element is incorporated into the Family Court Act § 1051(e) definition of severe abuse, and that Family Court properly excused diligent efforts here on a finding that they would be detrimental to the child's best interests.
cases.quote: Family Court may excuse diligent efforts when they are found to be detrimental to the best interests of the child

relevance.OUT-01: This is the current Court of Appeals statement of when the reunification obligation drops away: diligent efforts are excused, not merely deferred, once the court finds them detrimental to the child's best interests.

cases.holding: Reversing the dismissal of an abuse petition filed on behalf of a six-month-old who drowned, the Court held that a deceased child may be the subject of a Family Court Act article 10 abuse petition, because an adjudication that the parent abused or severely abused the child who died protects the surviving siblings, is admissible in a later proceeding to terminate parental rights, and preserves a judicial record of the circumstances of the death.
cases.quote: We thus reject the contention that a deceased child cannot be the subject of an abuse petition.

relevance.OUT-06: This is the controlling New York authority requiring that a child fatality be adjudicated rather than closed as moot, so that the facts and circumstances surrounding the child's death become a matter of record and the surviving siblings receive the protection of Social Services Law § 384-b.

cases.holding: Reversing in the Storar case, the Court held that although a parent or guardian may consent to medical treatment on behalf of an infant, the parent may not deny a child all treatment for a life-threatening condition even on religious grounds, and that the mother of a profoundly retarded man with the mental age of an infant therefore could not refuse the blood transfusions needed to keep him alive.
cases.quote: the courts may not permit a parent to deny a child all treatment for a condition which threatens his life

relevance.ACT-06: This is the Court of Appeals' statement of when the State may authorize immediate lifesaving medical care over a parent's objection, and it marks the boundary with Matter of Hofbauer: courts do not choose among reasonable treatments the parents have selected, but they will not allow a parent to withhold all treatment where the child's life is at stake.

notes: All 44 cases were retrieved from CourtListener and every quote was mechanically verified to be an exact substring of the retrieved majority-opinion text after whitespace and curly-quote normalization. No case or quotation was written from memory. The nine cases added in this pass were retrieved and read in this session; the 35 carried forward were retrieved and verified in the prior session and are reproduced unchanged.

RETRACTED: the prior brief's ICWA note asserting that no published New York appellate decision applies ICWA's substantive standards is false and is withdrawn. Matter of Baby Boy C., 27 A.D.3d 34 (1st Dep't 2005), retrieved and read in this session, squarely rejects the 'existing Indian family' exception, holds that ICWA's only threshold requirements are a child custody proceeding involving an Indian child, recognizes the tribe's independent interest under Holyfield, and remands for a hearing on the 25 U.S.C. sec. 1915 placement preferences and the good-cause exception. INP-11 now rests on that decision plus Holyfield. Matter of Landyn M. (Laquanna W.), 145 A.D.3d 520 (1st Dep't 2016), remains excluded because it declined to reach ICWA as unpreserved.

Added Matter of Baby Boy C. (cluster 5839166) for INP-11: it is the published New York appellate authority reaching ICWA's merits and it closes the only node that previously rested on a single federal case.

Added Matter of Ella B. (cluster 5679136) for INP-04 and DEC-05: the foundational New York holding that an indigent parent in a neglect proceeding is entitled to assigned counsel and must be affirmatively advised of that right. The prior pass omitted it for want of a quotable sentence; the quote used here is a complete, quote-mark-free clause from Chief Judge Fuld's opinion for the Court ('to be relinquished to the State without the opportunity for a hearing, with assigned counsel if the parent lacks the means to retain a lawyer'), verified as an exact substring. Note the disposition: the Court modified and remitted for a new adjudicatory and dispositional hearing rather than vacating the 1969 order outright.

Added Matter of Nassau County Dep't of Social Servs. ex rel. Dante M. v. Denise J. (cluster 2092873) for INP-07, DEC-03 and ACT-02: it is the leading New York causation authority holding that a newborn's positive toxicology alone cannot establish neglect, and it supplies the element DEC-03 previously lacked - the required link between a medical result and actual or imminent impairment. Practitioners should note the Court nonetheless affirmed on the other record evidence, so the case is a limit on inference, not a bar to a finding.

Added Duchesne v. Sugarman (cluster 350998) for INP-05, INP-12, DEC-04 and FAIL-02: the foundational Second Circuit family-integrity and section 1983 decision on which Tenenbaum and Southerland are built. It closes the gap identified by the verifier - the brief previously carried the descendants without the parent case.

Added Nicholson v. Scoppetta, 344 F.3d 154 (cluster 783602) for INP-12 and DEC-04: the Second Circuit decision that certified the questions answered by the New York Court of Appeals at 3 N.Y.3d 357. CORRECTION to the verifier's description: on CourtListener and in F.3d this decision is captioned Nicholson v. Scoppetta, not Nicholson v. Williams (Williams is the district court caption, 203 F.R.D. 153 (E.D.N.Y. 2001)). It is also a certification decision, not a merits holding; its statements of the federal emergency-removal standard are quotations of Tenenbaum v. Williams, 193 F.3d 581, and were therefore not used as the quote. The quote is the panel's own conclusion that the removals may raise serious federal constitutional questions but that state law comes first.

Added Matter of Marino S. (cluster 2017740) for DEC-05 and OUT-01: it supplies the derivative-findings holding that DEC-05 previously lacked and the diligent-efforts exception that OUT-01 previously omitted. CORRECTION: the official citation is 100 N.Y.2d 361 (2003), not 100 N.Y.3d 361 as the verifier wrote.

Added Matter of Dashawn W. (cluster 5642236) for OUT-01: the current Court of Appeals statement that Family Court may excuse diligent efforts on a finding that they would be detrimental to the child's best interests. CORRECTION to the verifier's description: Dashawn W. is not a derivative-neglect decision. Its holdings concern the meaning of 'circumstances evincing a depraved indifference to human life' under Social Services Law sec. 384-b(8)(a)(i) and the incorporation and excusal of the diligent-efforts element; derivative findings appear only in footnote 5, which quotes Marino S. The derivative-neglect authority in this brief is therefore Marino S., not Dashawn W.

Added Matter of Alijah C. (cluster 2224756) for OUT-06: the Court of Appeals holding that a deceased child may be the subject of an article 10 abuse petition, so that a fatality is adjudicated on the record rather than dismissed as moot and the surviving siblings obtain the protection of Social Services Law sec. 384-b. CORRECTION to the verifier's description: Alijah C. is not about the permanent-neglect planning requirement or the limits of the diligent-efforts obligation; it is about whether a petition may name a child who has died. It is mapped accordingly.

Added Matter of Storar (Eichner v. Dillon) (cluster 5684709) for ACT-06: ACT-06 previously carried only one case (Hofbauer). Storar is the Court of Appeals' statement of the converse rule - that a parent may not deny a child all treatment for a life-threatening condition, even on religious grounds - and the Court reversed to permit the blood transfusions. The CourtListener cluster is captioned Eichner v. Dillon because the Court decided the Eichner and Storar appeals in one opinion; the official New York Reports caption for the transfusion case is Matter of Storar. Matter of Philip M. (cluster 2065121) was also added to ACT-06 in the node map: its existing verified entry already carried an ACT-06 relevance sentence that the prior node map omitted.

No named authority failed verification: all eight authorities the verifier listed as missing were located on CourtListener, retrieved, read, and are included. Three of the eight carried inaccurate descriptions, corrected in the notes above (Marino S. reporter volume; Alijah C. subject matter; Dashawn W. subject matter), and one carried an inaccurate case name (Nicholson v. Williams / Nicholson v. Scoppetta).

Node-map capacity: six nodes are now at the six-case ceiling (DEC-03, DEC-05, ACT-02, OUT-01, OUT-02). OUT-02 was already full before this pass, so Marino S., Alijah C. and Dashawn W. could not be added there even though each bears on termination; they are mapped to OUT-01, OUT-06 and OUT-01 respectively, and counsel working a termination node should read OUT-01 and OUT-06 alongside OUT-02. No existing mapping was removed.

Differential/alternative response (DEC-06): New York has no statutory differential-response track comparable to other states. DEC-06 is mapped to the closest real authority: the OCFS Host Family Home preventive-services regulations upheld in Matter of Lawyers for Children (2025), voluntary placement under Social Services Law sec. 384-a as described in Matter of Michael B., and Nicholson's rejection of any blanket presumption favoring removal. Note the Lawyers for Children dissent would have held OCFS exceeded its rulemaking authority; the issue may reach the Court of Appeals.
Missing children from care: no New York appellate decision was found addressing children who go missing or abscond from foster placement. No case is offered on that point.

PMC-02 (OIG/Single Audit), PMC-03 (CAPTA Citizen Review Panels) and PMC-04 (federal Fatality Review Commission): no New York or Second Circuit decision construes any of these federal oversight mechanisms. These nodes are populated with the nearest genuinely on-point authority - Mark G. v. Sabol, the Marisol A. and Elisa W. systemic class actions, and Weisbrod-Moore and Doe on post-harm liability - and should be read as the accountability architecture actually available, not as construction of the federal statutes.

Standard-of-proof timing trap for the Central Register: Matter of Lee TT. v. Dowling (1996) required a fair preponderance only before dissemination to providers and licensing agencies; the 2020 amendments to Social Services Law sec. 422 (L 2020, ch 56, part R), effective January 1, 2022, made fair preponderance the general substantiation standard and added an irrebuttable presumption tied to article 10 outcomes. Matter of Jeter v. Poole (2024) holds those amendments are NOT retroactive to determinations rendered before January 1, 2022. Any SCR matter must be dated before the standard is chosen.

Mandated-reporter liability is narrower than Kimberly S.M. alone suggests. Matter of Catherine G. (2004) and Dolgas v. Wales (2023) hold there is no sec. 413 duty and no sec. 420(2) liability where the alleged abuser is not a 'parent or other person legally responsible' for the child - excluding siblings, teachers and other institutional caregivers. Read the three together.

Southerland v. City of New York: the CourtListener full text is the slip opinion with per-line numbering embedded in the body, so running prose from the body cannot be reproduced as an exact substring. The quote used is from footnote 15 of the majority opinion, which prints without line numbers. Note also that this cluster (681 F.3d 122) is the amended opinion superseding 652 F.3d 209 and 667 F.3d 87, which appear as separate CourtListener clusters.

Matter of Sheila G.: CourtListener opinion id 5536077 in this cluster is Judge Kaye's concurrence. The holding and quote here are taken from Chief Judge Cooke's lead opinion (id 5536076). Similarly, Matter of Jeter v. Poole contains a substantial dissent and Nicholson v. Scoppetta (2d Cir.) contains a dissent from the decision to certify; nothing from either was used.

Five recent decisions carried no official reporter citation in their CourtListener cluster and are given in slip form: Matter of Jamie J. (No. 118), Matter of Parker J. (No. 85), Matter of Jeter v. Poole (No. 82), Weisbrod-Moore v. Cayuga County (No. 7) and Matter of Lawyers for Children (No. CV-23-2341). Matter of Jamie J. is reported at 30 N.Y.3d 275 in print; that cite is not asserted because the cluster did not carry it.

Case names are given in New York Reports style ('Matter of ...'), which is how the deciding courts style them; CourtListener's cluster captions often read 'In re ...' or use the parties' names (e.g. 'In re Baby Boy C.' for Matter of Baby Boy C., 'In re Ella B.' for Matter of Ella B., 'In re Dashawn W.' for Matter of Dashawn W., 'Eichner v. Dillon' for Matter of Storar, 'Gregory B. v. Gregory F.' for Matter of Gregory B.). The URLs and cluster_ids resolve regardless.

Matter of Elizabeth C. (Omar C.) was technically academic by the time of decision, but the Second Department expressly applied the exception to the mootness doctrine, reached the merits, and reversed. It is a published merits holding, not dictum.

Nicholson v. Scoppetta, 3 N.Y.3d 357, answers questions certified by the Second Circuit in the federal Nicholson appeal now included in this brief at 344 F.3d 154; the underlying injunction is reported at 203 F.R.D. 153 (E.D.N.Y. 2001). The state-law rules cited in the brief come from the Court of Appeals answer, which is the binding New York authority.

Every 'key_cases' entry already present in the NY node files was keyword-matched noise - unemployment-insurance, tax-assessment and housing cases (Matter of Mantilla, Matter of Jensen v Commissioner of Labor, Matter of Carmody, Matter of First United Methodist Church, Matter of Aungst v Family Dollar, and others) with synthetic citations. None was retained. Two FOIL titles in those files (Matter of Prisoners' Legal Servs. and Matter of Appellate Advocates) are real Court of Appeals cases but concern correctional records, not child welfare; Matter of NYCLU v. City of Rochester is the better and more recent statement of the same FOIL rule and is used instead.

Coverage check after this pass: all 42 node ids are populated, each with between 2 and 6 cases; 44 distinct cases are returned. No node now rests on purely federal authority: INP-11, the last such node, now carries Matter of Baby Boy C. alongside Holyfield. The case count exceeds the 20-40 target band by four because the prior brief already stood at 35 and every addition here closes a specifically identified gap; none is padding.

Missing (for a later pass): Tenenbaum v. Williams, 193 F.3d 581 (2d Cir. 1999) — the most conspicuous omission. This is the Second Circuit's own articulation of the standard the brief's INP-12, DEC-04 and FAIL-02 nodes turn on: a child may not be seized without a court order absent objectively reasonable evidence of imminent danger; a Family Court order is the warrant equivalent; and even a justified emergency removal requires a prompt post-deprivation hearing. The brief's own notes concede that the federal Nicholson's statements of the emergency-removal standard are quotations OF Tenenbaum and that Southerland builds on it, yet Tenenbaum itself is absent. Verified on CourtListener (cluster 766396, 2d Cir., 1999-10-13).

Missing (for a later pass): Matter of Yolanda D., 88 N.Y.2d 790, 673 N.E.2d 1228, 651 N.Y.S.2d 1 (1996) — the Court of Appeals' leading definition of 'person legally responsible' under Family Court Act 1012(g), setting out the functional-equivalent-of-a-parent test and its factors. The brief's INP-01, INP-08 and DEC-01 nodes all depend on that boundary (Catherine G., Dolgas, Kimberly S.M.), but the brief supplies only Appellate Division applications and a sibling-specific Court of Appeals holding, never the controlling Court of Appeals test itself. Verified on CourtListener (cluster 2148810, N.Y., 1996-10-22).

Missing (for a later pass): Matter of Sanjivini K., 47 N.Y.2d 374, 391 N.E.2d 1316, 418 N.Y.S.2d 339 (1979) — the Court of Appeals holding that a child may not be kept from a fit parent, or parental rights curtailed, simply because the child has been in foster care a long time and the agency failed to work toward return; the State must establish a statutory ground, and prolonged placement of the agency's own making cannot supply it. Directly relevant to OUT-01 and OUT-02 and the necessary companion to Michael B. and Sheila G. Verified on CourtListener (cluster 5683527, N.Y., 1979-06-12).

Missing (for a later pass): Matter of Corey L v Martin L, 45 N.Y.2d 383, 380 N.E.2d 266, 408 N.Y.S.2d 439 (1978) — the Court of Appeals' foundational construction of the permanent-neglect ground, holding that the agency must prove both diligent efforts and the parent's failure substantially and continuously to maintain contact with OR plan for the future of the child although physically and financially able to do so. OUT-02 currently relies on Star Leslie W. and Sheila G. for the elements; Corey L is the decision they build on and is the better statement of the disjunctive contact-or-plan requirement. Verified on CourtListener (cluster 5683040, N.Y., 1978-07-13).

Missing (for a later pass): Kia P. v. McIntyre, 235 F.3d 749 (2d Cir. 2000) — the Second Circuit's treatment of a hospital hold on a newborn after a positive toxicology screen, addressing when a medical hold becomes a state seizure, the Fourth and Fourteenth Amendment analysis, and the procedural due process claim. It is the federal complement to Dante M./Denise J. at INP-07 and INP-12 and the brief has no authority at all on newborn hospital holds, a recurring New York City fact pattern. Verified on CourtListener (cluster 771505, 2d Cir., 2000-12-05).

Missing (for a later pass): Wilkinson ex rel. Wilkinson v. Russell, 182 F.3d 89 (2d Cir. 1999) — the circuit's standard for qualified immunity of caseworkers conducting child-abuse investigations, holding that an investigation offends due process only where it is so attenuated from any reasonable suspicion as to be arbitrary, and setting the deference owed to caseworkers acting under uncertainty. FAIL-02 currently states that caseworkers have only qualified immunity (via Cornejo) without supplying the content of that immunity, which is the question that actually decides these cases. Verified on CourtListener (cluster 764989, 2d Cir., 1999-06-17).
